text: Families should not be separated at the border, and immigration detention should be reserved for people who pose a genuine risk to public safety.
We should keep core clean air and water protections in place while speeding up permitting reviews, so that necessary projects move forward without weakening standards.
Housing assistance should be temporary and tied to work requirements, helping families get back on their feet without creating long-term reliance on government.
Addiction is a public health issue, so we should shift most drug enforcement spending toward treatment, recovery housing, and mental health care.
Abortion is the taking of an innocent human life, and governments have a moral duty to ban it nationwide and prosecute those who perform it.
Tax credit scholarships offer a sensible way to give families more options without dismantling the public school system that many communities still rely on.
Social Security should remain a safety net, but reforms must focus on trimming future benefit growth so the program does not crowd out other priorities.
We should abolish the current deportation system entirely and grant immediate citizenship to every undocumented person living in the country today.
Unelected health bureaucrats should be stripped of emergency powers entirely, because mandates crush small businesses and erode the freedoms our nation was founded upon.
We should keep nutrition assistance in the farm bill while adding modest work requirements, preserving the coalition that passes it and the safety net it funds.
Laws should be justified by secular reasons accessible to all citizens, since a diverse society cannot base policy on any single religious tradition.
Cutting benefits or privatizing Social Security should be off the table, and the program should instead expand to credit unpaid caregivers and restore student benefits.
Federal infrastructure spending should be slashed and returned to states, because Washington wastes money on bloated projects that local governments could build cheaper and faster.
Background checks at licensed dealers are reasonable, but extending them to private transfers between family members and friends goes too far.
Expanding housing vouchers so every eligible low-income household receives one would reduce homelessness and help families move to neighborhoods with better opportunities.
Voucher programs too often subsidize families already paying private tuition, so we should redirect those dollars toward underfunded public schools in low-income areas.
Paid leave policy works best when states and employers design their own approaches, since a single national program would ignore differences in local economies.
Lowering the eligibility age for government-run senior coverage would protect millions of older workers from the high costs of private insurance.
Transgender youth deserve access to gender-affirming care decided by families and doctors, and state legislatures should not override established medical guidance.
A national minimum of paid leave, with states free to build on it and small employers given hardship exemptions, balances family needs and business realities.
Every eligible citizen should be automatically registered and mailed a ballot for every election, making voting a guaranteed right rather than an obstacle course.
Expanding charter schools and education savings accounts would give families in struggling districts more options while pressuring traditional public schools to improve.
Labor law should be strengthened with meaningful fines for employers who retaliate against workers trying to form a union.
We should break up the largest corporations in every concentrated industry, because unchecked corporate power undermines democracy, crushes workers, and exploits consumers.
We must phase out factory farming entirely, because concentrated animal operations poison rural water, abuse animals, and drive climate change for corporate profit.
Red flag laws can be worthwhile if they include strong due process protections, such as prompt court hearings and penalties for false petitions.
Higher education is a fundamental right, so we should guarantee free tuition, living stipends, and debt-free degrees just as we guarantee public schooling.
We should keep drug possession a crime but give first-time offenders the option of court-supervised treatment, while maintaining tough penalties for dealers.
Regulators should give special attention to low-income communities near highways and factories, which have long borne a disproportionate share of pollution.
We should dramatically shrink the prison system and close most facilities, because mass incarceration is a racist institution that destroys communities rather than protecting them.
Police departments need more funding, more officers, and stronger legal protections, because a society that hesitates to enforce its laws invites disorder and crime.
Paid family leave strengthens families and the economy by keeping parents attached to the workforce, so we should establish a national program covering all employees.
We should be cautious about strict emissions targets that disadvantage domestic manufacturers while major competitors abroad continue increasing their own emissions.
Stronger tenant protections and a right to counsel in eviction cases would keep many struggling families from ever losing their homes.
Inclusive curricula that acknowledge LGBTQ history and families help all students feel safe and should be a normal part of public education.
We must ban all new oil, gas, and coal projects immediately and phase out fossil fuels entirely within a decade to avert climate catastrophe.
We should phase in paid family leave gradually, starting with lower-income workers and small-business subsidies, and evaluate the results before expanding it further.
Health agencies should have expanded, permanent authority to require masks, vaccines, and closures, because protecting the most vulnerable outweighs claims of individual inconvenience.
Public health mandates must be paired with guaranteed paid sick leave and income support, because collective safety should never depend on workers sacrificing their livelihoods.
Faith-based groups can receive public funds for social services if the programs are open to everyone and the money does not pay for worship.
We should slash the regulatory red tape strangling nuclear power and let private companies build reactors quickly, without federal bureaucrats dictating every step of the process.
Captive-audience meetings and corporate union-busting campaigns should be outlawed outright, with executives held personally liable when companies illegally suppress organizing.
We should significantly increase public investment in buses and rail, because reliable transit reduces traffic, cuts emissions, and connects workers to jobs.
Endless military expansion fuels war rather than preventing it, and we should dismantle the war economy by sharply cutting arms purchases and ending foreign interventions.
The federal immigration enforcement agency should be dismantled and all deportations halted, with every undocumented resident granted immediate permanent legal status.
Immigration detention centers should be shut down permanently, because caging people for seeking a better life is a fundamental violation of human rights.
We should require universal background checks on all gun sales, including private and online transactions, to close loopholes that let dangerous people obtain firearms.
We should create a clear path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked here for years and contributed to their communities.
Strict photo ID laws block more eligible voters than fraudsters, so states should accept signed affidavits from voters who lack the required documents.
Trade policy must put domestic manufacturers first, even if that means sweeping tariffs and abandoning agreements that have shipped our factory jobs overseas.
Wealthy nations owe a moral debt to the global poor, and we should dramatically increase foreign aid to at least one percent of national income.
We should forgive a meaningful portion of federal student debt for middle- and lower-income borrowers, since rising tuition was largely beyond their control.
Emergency rental assistance should be targeted to low-income families at immediate risk of eviction, a modest cost that prevents far more expensive homelessness later.
We should strengthen emissions standards for power plants and vehicles because the costs of unchecked climate change far exceed the costs of regulation.
Employers should be required to verify workers' legal status electronically, since reducing the job magnet is one of the most effective ways to discourage illegal entry.
Government homeless programs have wasted billions with nothing to show for it, and that money should be cut and redirected to police and private charities.
We should offer targeted loan relief for low-income borrowers who were defrauded or have repaid for decades, while avoiding broad cancellation for high earners.
Temporary mandates can be justified in genuine emergencies, but they should require legislative approval after a set period and include reasonable medical and religious exemptions.
We should offer means-tested scholarships for low-income students in persistently failing districts while maintaining stable funding for the public schools most children attend.
Insurers should face strict limits on out-of-pocket costs and denials, and federal subsidies should grow until no family spends more than a small share of income on premiums.
Mail voting should be available to anyone who requests it, paired with signature verification and a clear process for voters to fix rejected ballots.
We should reject any federal paid leave program, because new payroll taxes and expanded entitlements would shrink paychecks, kill jobs, and grow an already bloated government.
The national debt is a moral failure that steals from our children, and we should slash federal spending across every agency until the budget is balanced.
We need universal rent control and a ban on corporate ownership of single-family homes, because landlords and investors are profiting from a basic necessity.
Every public college and university should be completely tuition-free for all students, funded by higher taxes on the wealthiest households and largest corporations.
We should keep core health, safety, and environmental rules while periodically reviewing older regulations and retiring those that no longer serve a clear purpose.
Student loans should be dischargeable in bankruptcy like other consumer debt, giving struggling borrowers the same protections available to everyone else.
We should strengthen antitrust enforcement to block mergers that reduce competition, raise prices for consumers, and give a few large firms excessive market power.
Homelessness is driven mainly by addiction and personal choices, so taxpayers should not fund free housing for people who refuse treatment or work.
Pretrial detention should be abolished entirely, since jailing people who have not been convicted of any crime violates the presumption of innocence and devastates poor families.
Cashless bail and early release programs put dangerous criminals back into communities, so we must end them and keep accused offenders detained until trial.
We should set binding targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions substantially by 2035, backed by strong incentives for renewables and electric vehicles.
A larger share of highway funding should be shifted toward bus lanes, rail, and bike connections to give people real alternatives to driving.
Means-tested premium assistance paired with stronger price transparency rules would make coverage more affordable while keeping overall federal spending under control.
We must substantially defund police departments and reinvest that money in housing, healthcare, and education, because policing cannot fix the root causes of crime.
Families should be free to take their tax dollars to any private, religious, or home school without permission or interference from teachers' unions or state officials.
We should strengthen limits on power plant and vehicle emissions, because the health and climate costs of pollution far exceed the price of compliance.
We should expand shipbuilding, missile defense, and troop levels immediately, since a weakened military betrays our soldiers and emboldens hostile regimes worldwide.
Diversity offices and preference programs divide Americans by race, so public funding for them should be eliminated across every university and government agency.
Physical barriers make sense in some urban stretches, but most funding should go toward surveillance technology and screening at ports where most contraband actually enters.
Small businesses deserve exemptions from many compliance requirements, since paperwork designed for large corporations can overwhelm owners with limited staff and resources.
Armed police should be removed from schools, traffic stops, and mental health calls entirely, because their presence escalates harm against marginalized communities.
Social media companies have a responsibility to curb hate speech and coordinated harassment, and modest regulation should ensure they actually enforce their own policies.
Absentee ballots should remain available, but voters ought to request them each election and include identification details so signatures alone are not the only check.
Borrowers who chose expensive degrees with little market value must bear the full consequences of their decisions rather than expecting any bailout from the public.
Large corporations should pay a somewhat higher tax rate, because many currently pay far less than ordinary workers as a share of income.
We should guarantee every resident a universal basic income high enough to live on, ending poverty as a matter of right rather than charity.
Charter schools can be a useful option when they meet the same transparency and testing requirements as traditional public schools and close if they underperform.
We should repeal prevailing wage mandates and union labor requirements on public works, since they inflate costs and leave taxpayers paying far more for every mile of road.
Paid family leave is a basic human right, and we should guarantee every worker at least six months at full pay, funded by taxing corporations and the wealthy.
Climate regulations are destroying good-paying energy jobs, and we must withdraw from international climate agreements that hand control of our economy to foreign bureaucrats.
Transit fares should stay affordable through targeted discounts for low-income riders, while general fares continue covering a reasonable portion of operating costs.
Laws that criminalize sleeping or camping in public punish people for being poor and should be repealed entirely in every city.
Highway expansion should be halted and those funds redirected to fare-free public transit, because building more roads only deepens car dependence and accelerates climate breakdown.
Same-day registration should be standard nationwide, so that eligible citizens are not turned away simply because they missed an arbitrary paperwork deadline.
Holiday displays on public property are acceptable when they include multiple traditions, balancing respect for heritage with fairness toward citizens of other beliefs.
We should narrow liability protections for tech companies that act more like publishers, while keeping government out of day-to-day content decisions.
We should abolish federal wetland rules on private farmland entirely, because a puddle in a farmer's field is private property, not a matter for bureaucrats.
Bail reform has gone too far in some places, so judges should regain discretion to detain defendants who pose a clear risk to public safety.
Public funding for abortion could be limited to low-income women in cases of rape, incest, or medical risk, as a workable compromise.
Lessons on sexual orientation and gender identity belong in later grades, and parents should be notified and allowed to opt their children out.
Raising payroll taxes to rescue Social Security would punish working Americans, so benefits must be cut substantially and the retirement age raised well above current levels.
Regulatory agencies need more funding and staff to enforce existing consumer protection and workplace safety laws that companies too often ignore without consequence.
We should abolish federal restrictions on firearm ownership entirely, including background check mandates, because law-abiding citizens should never need government permission to defend themselves.
Every state should offer no-excuse mail voting and secure drop boxes, because convenient options raise turnout without any meaningful increase in fraud.
A modest safety net is appropriate, but we should favor temporary assistance that moves recipients toward self-sufficiency over open-ended government support.
Taxpayers who never attended college should not be forced to pay off loans that other adults voluntarily signed, so federal debt cancellation must be stopped entirely.
A sensible approach would require dominant platforms to allow data portability and interoperability, increasing competition without the disruption of forcibly splitting companies apart.
Any cut to the defense budget invites aggression abroad, so we should fund our armed forces generously before spending a single dollar on domestic programs.
Nuclear power should be part of a diverse clean energy mix, paired with expanded renewables and a firm federal plan for long-term waste storage.
Opening foreign markets through trade agreements will help farmers more than new subsidies, so we should prioritize export access over domestic spending programs.
Antitrust enforcement should consider harms to workers, small businesses, and privacy, not just short-term prices, when evaluating the conduct of major tech companies.
Social Security's funding gap should be closed with a balanced package that modestly raises the payroll tax cap and gradually increases the full retirement age.
Any paid leave expansion should exempt small businesses and avoid new payroll taxes, so that supporting families does not come at the cost of jobs.
Dominant platforms should be prohibited from favoring their own products over competitors' offerings, since that practice unfairly squeezes smaller businesses that depend on them.
Gradually raising the gas tax and indexing it to inflation, paired with a mileage fee for electric vehicles, would fund highways fairly without major new borrowing.
Union-elected worker representatives should hold half the seats on corporate boards, because labor creates the wealth and deserves equal power over company decisions.
Legalizing marijuana was a serious mistake, and we should reverse it before normalized drug use further erodes family stability, public safety, and the work ethic.
Younger workers should have the option to invest a portion of their payroll taxes in personal accounts while current retirees keep their promised benefits.
Every new rule imposed on employers kills jobs and stifles innovation, so we should freeze all new regulations and dismantle the existing burdens on business.
Medicare and Social Security should be protected from benefit cuts, with their funding gaps closed by asking the wealthiest Americans to pay more.
Pairing a modest minimum wage increase with tax relief for small businesses would help low-income workers without placing an excessive burden on employers.
Military spending has grown faster than our actual security needs, so modest reductions paired with stronger oversight of contractors would serve taxpayers better.
Families arriving at the border should not be detained or separated, and alternatives such as case management and check-ins should be used instead.
Public health officials need the authority to issue mask and vaccine requirements during outbreaks, because individual choices can endanger vulnerable neighbors.
Cutting foreign aid undermines diplomacy and public health, so we should restore funding levels and commit to steady, predictable support for developing nations.
Foreign aid is a small share of the budget that delivers outsized benefits, and modest increases would strengthen both humanitarian outcomes and international goodwill.
Qualified immunity must be abolished entirely, so that officers who violate people's civil rights face the same legal consequences as any other citizen.
We should gradually trim the defense budget by cutting unnecessary weapons programs and shifting some of those savings toward diplomacy, veterans' care, and domestic needs.
Regulators should focus on narrow, targeted remedies for specific anticompetitive conduct by tech firms instead of pursuing broad structural changes to the industry.
Farm regulations should be streamlined and reviewed for cost, so family operations are not buried in paperwork designed with large industrial producers in mind.
Legal immigration should shift toward a merit-based system that favors applicants with skills, education, and English proficiency over extended family connections.
A modest, gradually rising carbon fee with revenue returned to households as rebates would reduce emissions without raising the overall cost of living.
Homelessness programs should be expanded only where independent audits show they actually move people into stable housing, with funding tied to measurable results.
Paid leave mandates would devastate small businesses, which cannot afford to cover absent workers, so lawmakers should repeal existing state requirements rather than add new ones.
Our nation should withdraw from international trade bodies that override our sovereignty and impose steep tariffs on any country that refuses to trade on fair terms.
Housing First programs should be expanded, because giving people stable housing before requiring treatment has proven more effective than making them earn a bed.
We should decriminalize possession of all drugs for personal use, because the war on drugs has caused far more harm than the drugs themselves.
Sectoral bargaining should set binding wage and benefit standards across entire industries, so every worker is covered by a union contract regardless of employer.
Rather than raising the minimum wage, we should eliminate it and cut regulations so that entry-level jobs multiply and young workers can gain experience.
We should ban parent-driven book removals entirely and guarantee every student access to diverse literature, including stories about race, sexuality, and gender.
Defense budgets should be set by a multiyear strategic plan, increasing in areas like cyber defense while trimming duplicative programs that no longer meet current threats.
We should reduce the deficit through a balanced package that combines modest spending cuts with targeted revenue increases, phased in as the economy allows.
Public funds should not pay for elective abortions, since many taxpayers hold sincere moral objections to the procedure.
All nonmedical vaccine exemptions should be eliminated nationwide, because refusing vaccination is not a personal choice when it threatens the lives of others.
The absence of universal paid leave is a national disgrace that lets corporations exploit working families, and only a generous, fully public program can end it.
Teachers deserve significantly higher salaries and stronger union protections, since chronic underpayment is driving experienced educators out of the profession.
Competition from charter and private schools pushes public schools to improve, so states should allow more funding to follow students to the schools parents choose.
No nation that votes against us or harbors hostility toward our values should receive a single cent of aid, and most programs should be abolished.
Abortion should be legal through fetal viability, and states should not impose medically unnecessary waiting periods or mandatory counseling requirements.
Penalties for illegally firing union organizers should be increased, while employers should retain the right to share their views on unionization during campaigns.
We should cap annual growth in discretionary spending and reduce the deficit gradually, relying mainly on spending restraint rather than new taxes.
Religious organizations should lose their automatic tax exemptions, because subsidizing churches forces all taxpayers, including nonbelievers, to support institutions they reject.
Criminalizing homelessness through encampment sweeps is cruel and must end, and every unhoused person should receive permanent housing immediately with no conditions attached.
Public investment and tax incentives should accelerate the shift to renewable energy, paired with stronger standards that phase down fossil fuel use over time.
We should allow limited, means-tested school choice programs for low-income families while maintaining stable funding for traditional public schools in those districts.
Abortion should be restricted after the first trimester, with exceptions only for rape, incest, or serious threats to the mother's life.
Teacher pay should rise gradually, paired with reformed evaluation systems that reward effective instruction and make it easier to address persistent underperformance.
Housing is a human right, and the government should guarantee a permanent home to every person, with no conditions on sobriety or employment.
A public insurance option offered alongside private plans would increase competition without forcing anyone to give up coverage they already like.
Civilians have no need for military-style firearms or high-capacity magazines, and the country should drastically shrink its civilian gun supply to match other wealthy democracies.
Bail decisions should rely on validated risk assessments, detaining defendants who pose real danger while releasing low-risk people who simply cannot afford payment.
Schools should refocus on core subjects like reading, math, and civics, and spend less class time on social and emotional programming.
Regulatory agencies have become unaccountable engines of overreach, and we should abolish many of them so that free markets can discipline businesses instead.
We should maintain current police funding while requiring body cameras and clear use-of-force standards, so communities get both public safety and accountability.
We should dismantle most federal welfare programs and return responsibility for helping the poor to families, churches, and local charities.
Massive police budgets entrench a system built on control and punishment, and they should be dramatically reduced in favor of care-based public safety.
Nuclear energy deserves a larger role alongside natural gas because it provides steady baseload power that intermittent renewables cannot yet match on their own.
Platform companies should be legally barred from both operating marketplaces and selling products on them, separating these functions as we once did with railroads.
We should keep corporate tax rates low and competitive with other developed nations so that companies invest and hire here rather than abroad.
Schools should respect a student's request for privacy about gender identity unless the student agrees to involve their family or safety requires it.
Cities should be allowed to open supervised consumption sites, since the evidence shows they prevent overdose deaths and connect users to treatment.
Public schools should teach about world religions objectively and allow voluntary student-led prayer, while staff refrain from leading or endorsing any particular faith.
Before raising any taxes, we should first cut wasteful spending, because government ought to prove it uses current revenue responsibly.
We should streamline permitting for energy and infrastructure projects, because lengthy environmental reviews delay construction for years without meaningfully improving outcomes.
We should increase police funding modestly while keeping firm sentencing standards, because a visible law enforcement presence deters most crime.
All drug offenses should be decriminalized and every person imprisoned for them released immediately, with their records erased and reparations paid to affected communities.
We should phase in tax changes gradually and review their results regularly, adjusting rates based on evidence about growth, revenue, and fairness.
Expanding antitrust powers to target tech platforms would invite endless government meddling, and we should repeal regulations rather than create new ones.
Immigration detention should be abolished entirely, because locking up people for seeking safety or a better life is a violation of basic human rights.
Permitting rules for roads, pipelines, and power lines should be streamlined with firm deadlines, since lengthy reviews add costs without meaningfully improving environmental outcomes.
We should ban public funding for charter and private schools entirely and fully nationalize school financing to guarantee equal resources for every child.
We should extend licenses for existing nuclear plants that pass rigorous safety reviews while funding pilot projects for smaller advanced reactors before committing to large-scale expansion.
Ending legacy and donor preferences alongside race-based ones would create a fairer admissions system that both critics and supporters of affirmative action could accept.
Parents deserve a voice in schools, but curriculum decisions should rest primarily with educators and experts rather than with vocal groups of objecting parents.
Workers caring for a newborn or seriously ill relative should not have to choose between their paycheck and their family, which is why paid leave belongs in law.
We should ban permanent replacement of strikers, legalize solidarity strikes, and guarantee every worker an unrestricted right to withhold labor without fear of retaliation.
We should pair stronger border enforcement with an earned path to legal status for long-term residents who pass background checks and pay any back taxes.
Users who are suspended or banned deserve a clear explanation and a fair appeals process, since vague moderation rules too easily chill legitimate political debate.
Public-private partnerships offering tax credits for including some affordable units in new developments can expand supply while sharing costs between government and builders.
Homelessness policy should combine expanded shelter capacity and housing programs with reasonable enforcement of public camping rules, phased in gradually and evaluated for results.
Emergency relief deserves steady funding, but long-term development aid should be conditioned on recipient governments meeting clear anti-corruption benchmarks over time.
Stronger financial regulations, including higher capital requirements for banks, are needed to prevent risky practices that can trigger crises and harm ordinary families.
We should end every subsidy to fossil fuel industries and redirect those funds into a fully renewable grid and reparations for frontline communities.
Government should openly acknowledge God in its laws, courts, and ceremonies, because a society that abandons faith inevitably loses its moral foundation.
Mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenses should be repealed, because they have filled prisons with nonviolent offenders without reducing drug use.
Laws restricting abortion are an attack on human rights, and all existing bans, gestational limits, and parental consent rules should be repealed.
No foreign government or global institution should have any say over our trade rules, and unelected international panels should never be allowed to overrule our courts.
Voter ID requirements are a deliberate tool of voter suppression and should be repealed everywhere, since in-person impersonation fraud is virtually nonexistent.
We must dramatically increase military spending, because overwhelming strength is the only language our adversaries understand and the surest guarantee of peace.
Government-run transit agencies are inherently wasteful and unaccountable, so we should privatize them completely and end the union contracts that drive costs sky-high.
Climate policy should rely on innovation and private investment rather than heavy regulation that raises energy costs for working families and small businesses.
Conservation programs should offer farmers voluntary payments for practices like cover cropping, protecting soil and water without imposing mandates that strain thin profit margins.
Farm subsidies should be capped and means-tested so support flows mainly to small and mid-sized operations rather than the largest agribusinesses.
We should protect contracting programs for minority-owned businesses, because discrimination in lending and networks still keeps many qualified firms from competing fairly.
Reducing police budgets would be a mistake, but some new money should go toward body cameras and training that strengthen public trust in officers.
We should expand foreign aid for global health, clean water, and education, because these investments save lives and build lasting stability abroad.
Agricultural immigration reform should pair a legal path for long-term farmworkers with an updated verification system, giving growers stable labor and enforcement real credibility.
We should keep the current mix of private and public insurance while gradually expanding subsidies for low-income families and capping the most expensive prescription drug prices.
The rising national debt threatens future growth, so we should trim federal programs and encourage private investment instead of expanding government borrowing.
Transit must remain fully public and unionized, and any attempt to privatize routes should be rejected as a giveaway that harms workers and riders.
We must slash military spending drastically and redirect those hundreds of billions toward universal health care, housing, and climate action that truly protect people.
Government should get out of the housing market entirely, abolishing rent control and public housing so private owners and builders can meet demand freely.
Unions helped build the middle class, and we should make it easier for workers to organize by allowing majority sign-up as an alternative to drawn-out elections.
Immigration levels should be adjusted gradually based on labor market needs, expanding visas in sectors with shortages while keeping overall numbers predictable and manageable.
We should pursue an all-of-the-above energy strategy that keeps natural gas as a bridge fuel while gradually expanding renewable and nuclear capacity.
Benefit spending should be held in check through stronger fraud prevention and eligibility verification, so limited funds reach people who truly need them.
Human life begins at conception, so abortion should be prohibited in all circumstances, and the law must protect every unborn child without exception.
Cutting police funding is a reckless experiment that has fueled crime waves, and cities must restore every dollar and give officers the full backing they deserve.
Private insurance should remain the backbone of our system, with targeted tax credits helping people afford coverage rather than an expanding government program.
Health mandates should be targeted to high-risk settings like hospitals and nursing homes rather than applied broadly, with clear data-driven criteria for lifting them.
Platforms should be free to set their own rules, but they ought to apply them transparently and consistently rather than disproportionately targeting conservative users.
Nutrition assistance should be protected from cuts and work requirements, and we should expand incentives that let recipients buy fresh produce from local farms.
We believe bodily autonomy is absolute, so no politician or court should ever have the power to force anyone to remain pregnant.
Private lenders and debt servicers should be removed entirely from higher education, since profiting from student debt exploits young people seeking opportunity.
We should pair modest rate cuts with closing narrow loopholes, keeping overall revenue roughly stable while making the tax code simpler for everyone.
A flatter tax code with fewer brackets and deductions would be simpler and fairer, even if some modest progressivity remains to protect lower earners.
Drug courts work well, but they function best when backed by the real threat of jail time for those who refuse to comply with treatment.
Government-mandated paid family leave is an unjustified burden on employers, and decisions about leave benefits should be left entirely to private businesses and their workers.
Enforcement agencies need more resources to audit large corporations, since aggressive tax avoidance shifts the burden onto small businesses and families.
Block-granting public health programs to the states would control federal spending and allow more flexible, locally tailored approaches to covering low-income residents.
Employers should recruit broadly from diverse communities and audit their hiring for bias, while making final decisions on qualifications rather than demographic targets.
Public education should be free from universal preschool through college, funded by steep tax increases on the wealthiest individuals and corporations.
Schools should teach respect for all families in age-appropriate ways while giving parents clear information about the curriculum and reasonable opportunities to review it.
Religious business owners should never be compelled by the government to participate in or provide services for ceremonies that violate their convictions.
Abortion is essential health care and should be available on demand at any stage of pregnancy, without government restrictions of any kind.
Gender-affirming care for minors should remain available but require thorough psychological evaluation, parental consent, and careful clinical standards before any medical treatment begins.
Federal and state governments should jointly fund tuition-free community college for students who meet income limits, while four-year degrees remain partly paid by families.
Clean energy tax credits should continue but be phased down over time and targeted at technologies that are not yet commercially competitive.
Borrowing to fund infrastructure, education, and clean energy is a sound investment, because these programs strengthen the economy that ultimately repays the debt.
The government should guarantee free comprehensive care for every resident regardless of immigration status, including dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care.
Housing, food, and healthcare are human rights, and government should guarantee them to all, funded by aggressive taxes on great concentrations of wealth.
Regulators should block more acquisitions by dominant tech firms, since buying up emerging rivals has steadily reduced competition and consumer choice.
We should protect benefits for current and near retirees while phasing in small, predictable changes to both revenues and benefits for younger workers.
Religious business owners and charities must never be forced by the state to violate their sincerely held beliefs, whatever antidiscrimination laws may demand.
Blanket legal immunity lets platforms ignore the real-world harm they enable, so we should make them fully liable for the hateful and false content they host.
Public-sector unions should be abolished entirely, because government employees bargaining against taxpayers creates an unaccountable conflict of interest that bloats budgets.
Comprehensive health and sex education should be the default in schools, with opt-outs available rather than a requirement for parental permission before every lesson.
Bail reform has gone too far in some places, and judges should have more discretion to detain defendants who pose a clear risk.
Environmental review laws should be gutted for infrastructure projects, because years of lawsuits and paperwork are strangling construction and mainly serve activists rather than the public.
Every loophole and offshore haven that lets corporations dodge taxes must be shut down completely, with harsh penalties for executives who exploit them.
Qualified immunity is essential for officers, and stripping it away would leave police afraid to act decisively when communities need them most.
Rather than deleting most disputed posts, platforms should rely mainly on context labels and reduced amplification, reserving removal for threats, fraud, and illegal material.
We should maintain stable police funding rather than cutting it, since reliable staffing and response times matter most to working families in high-crime neighborhoods.
Businesses forced to close under emergency health orders should receive compensation, so that public safety measures do not place the entire burden on owners and workers.
Breaking up large tech firms would hand bureaucrats sweeping control over private enterprise, which is a far greater threat to freedom than any company's size.
We should encourage adoption and support crisis pregnancy centers so that women facing unplanned pregnancies have real alternatives to abortion.
Public safety is the first duty of government, so police departments should receive whatever funding they need before a single dollar goes to other programs.
We should fund transit expansion where ridership data justify it, while requiring agencies to meet clear performance and cost benchmarks to keep receiving support.
Racial preferences insult the very people they claim to help, and merit alone should determine who gets admitted, hired, or awarded public contracts.
Some regulation protects public safety, but we should trim duplicative rules and speed up permitting so businesses can grow without needless delays.
Our nation should maintain the largest and most advanced military on earth, regardless of cost, because national security is the first duty of government.
Medical decisions belong entirely to individuals and families, so no employer, school, or government agency should ever be allowed to require vaccination as a condition of participation.
Private property owners, not distant regulators, should decide how their land is used, and wetland and endangered species rules routinely trample that fundamental right.
Doctors should be able to provide abortion care without fear of prosecution, and clinics need protection from harassment and obstruction.
Cash bail should be largely eliminated, because jailing people simply for being poor punishes them before any conviction and does little for safety.
The federal minimum wage has fallen far behind the cost of living, so we should raise it substantially and index it to inflation afterward.
Supervised injection sites and needle exchanges send the message that drug abuse is acceptable, so we should shut them down and enforce existing laws.
We need legally binding diversity requirements for universities and large employers, because voluntary efforts have failed to undo systemic racism built into these institutions.
Cities should pair mental health responders with police on certain emergency calls, rather than either replacing officers entirely or leaving them to handle everything alone.
We should cap executive pay at a fixed multiple of the lowest wage in each company, forcing corporations to lift up their lowest-paid workers.
